explanation: Both weigh 7.26 kg, which is 16 pounds. The hammer flies much farther because the thrower spins with it on a wire about 1.2 m long before letting go.

claims.text: Under World Athletics rules, the men's hammer (head, wire and handle together) and the men's shot have the same specified weight.
The men's hammer and the men's shot each weigh 7.26 kg.
7.26 kg is 16 pounds (16 lb is 7.257 kg).
The men's hammer, measured from the handle to the far side of the head, is about 1.2 metres long.
Hammer throwers turn several times inside the circle before releasing, which lets the hammer travel much farther than a put shot.

evidence.restatement: World Athletics sets one minimum mass, 7.26 kg, for both the senior men's shot and the complete senior men's hammer (head plus wire plus grip).

claimResults.note: Answered True cold. Both implements are the traditional 16 lb weight; the hammer's mass is specified for the assembled implement. Counterintuitive key, carried by direct certain confirmation under memo 18.

evidence.restatement: The senior men's shot and the senior men's hammer are each specified at 7.26 kg.

claimResults.note: World Athletics technical rules (shot put and hammer specifications).
Pure conversion: 16 lb = 7.257 kg, rounded to the rulebook's 7.26 kg.

evidence.restatement: The men's hammer may be at most 121.5 cm long overall, measured from the inside of the grip to the far side of the head, so roughly 1.2 m.

claimResults.note: Rule maximum is 121.5 cm; 'about 1.2 metres' holds.

evidence.restatement: Throwers make three or four turns in the circle before letting the hammer go, and it lands far beyond a shot put distance (world records about 86 m against about 23 m).

claimResults.note: Correct; the spin plus the long lever is why hammer distances dwarf shot distances.

issues.note: The explanation says the thrower spins 'on a wire about 1.2 m long'; the 1.2 m is the whole implement (grip to far side of head), and the wire alone is shorter. Claim c4 is worded correctly; the explanation could say 'on the end of a wire, about 1.2 m from grip to head'.

evidence.restatement: Senior men throw a 7.26 kg shot and a 7.26 kg hammer (head plus wire plus handle), so the two implements are specified at one weight.

claimResults.note: Rival test: 'weighs the same' could be doubted for real implements, since rules give minimum weights and makers tolerate small excesses; but the specified weight is identical, and the claim says so. Younger men's grades (6 kg and 5 kg) also pair shot and hammer at equal weights, so no age-group reading breaks it. Women's are 4 kg each, outside the stem anyway. The result confirms 7.26 kg for the senior men's hammer; my search did not retrieve the official rule text, so this rests on knowledge plus check A's evidence.
